title: Electronics II
source_note: Standard second electronics course building on PHY208 (Electronics I): operational amplifiers, feedback, oscillators, active filters, power supplies, and an introduction to digital electronics, as typically taught in NUC-aligned Nigerian physics programmes.

questions.question: An ideal operational amplifier is characterised by which of the following properties?
options: Infinite input impedance, zero output impedance, and infinite open-loop gain
Zero input impedance and infinite output impedance
Finite gain of exactly 1 with no feedback
Infinite bandwidth only, with finite gain
questions.correct_answer: Infinite input impedance, zero output impedance, and infinite open-loop gain
questions.explanation: An ideal op-amp has infinite input impedance (draws no input current), zero output impedance, and infinite open-loop voltage gain, along with infinite bandwidth.

questions.question: In the 'virtual short' concept used to analyse an ideal op-amp with negative feedback, it is assumed that:
options: The voltage at the inverting and non-inverting inputs are equal
Current flows freely between the two input terminals
The two inputs are physically connected by a wire
questions.correct_answer: The voltage at the inverting and non-inverting inputs are equal
questions.explanation: Due to the very high open-loop gain and negative feedback, the op-amp drives its output so that V+ ≈ V-, a 'virtual short' with no actual current flowing between the inputs.

questions.question: For an inverting amplifier with input resistor R1 and feedback resistor Rf, the closed-loop voltage gain is:
questions.correct_answer: Av = -Rf/R1
questions.explanation: The inverting amplifier gain is Av = -Rf/R1, with the negative sign indicating a 180-degree phase inversion between input and output.

questions.question: For a non-inverting amplifier with feedback resistor Rf and ground resistor R1, the closed-loop voltage gain is:
questions.correct_answer: Av = 1 + Rf/R1
questions.explanation: In the non-inverting amplifier configuration, the closed-loop gain is Av = 1 + Rf/R1, and the output is in phase with the input.

questions.question: A unity-gain buffer (voltage follower) op-amp circuit is used primarily to:
options: Amplify the input signal by a large factor
Provide high input impedance and low output impedance for impedance matching, with gain of 1
Invert the phase of the input signal
questions.correct_answer: Provide high input impedance and low output impedance for impedance matching, with gain of 1
questions.explanation: The voltage follower has the output directly fed back to the inverting input, giving unity gain while isolating a high-impedance source from a low-impedance load.

questions.question: A summing amplifier (adder) built with an op-amp produces an output that is:
options: The product of the input voltages
The weighted sum (with inversion) of several input voltages, scaled by their respective resistor ratios
Equal to only the largest input voltage
The average of the input voltages without scaling
questions.correct_answer: The weighted sum (with inversion) of several input voltages, scaled by their respective resistor ratios
questions.explanation: In an inverting summing amplifier, Vout = -Rf*(V1/R1 + V2/R2 + ...), giving a scaled, inverted sum of the input voltages.

questions.question: An op-amp integrator circuit uses a feedback capacitor instead of a resistor, producing an output that is proportional to:
options: The derivative of the input voltage with respect to time
The time integral of the input voltage
The square of the input voltage
The input voltage with no phase change
questions.correct_answer: The time integral of the input voltage
questions.explanation: An op-amp integrator produces Vout = -(1/RC) * integral of Vin dt, so the output voltage is proportional to the running integral of the input.

questions.question: An op-amp differentiator circuit uses an input capacitor and feedback resistor, producing an output proportional to:
options: The time integral of the input voltage
The rate of change (derivative) of the input voltage
The reciprocal of the input voltage
questions.correct_answer: The rate of change (derivative) of the input voltage
questions.explanation: The differentiator gives Vout = -RC * (dVin/dt), producing an output proportional to how fast the input voltage is changing.

questions.question: Negative feedback applied to an amplifier generally results in:
options: Reduced gain but improved bandwidth, stability, and reduced distortion
No change in gain but increased noise
questions.correct_answer: Reduced gain but improved bandwidth, stability, and reduced distortion
questions.explanation: Negative feedback trades a reduction in overall gain for significant improvements in bandwidth, gain stability, linearity, and reduced distortion and noise.

questions.question: For sustained oscillation to occur in a feedback oscillator circuit, the Barkhausen criterion requires that:
options: The loop gain magnitude equals 1 and the total phase shift around the loop is 0 (or a multiple of 360 degrees)
The loop gain be less than 1 at all frequencies
The amplifier must have infinite bandwidth
questions.correct_answer: The loop gain magnitude equals 1 and the total phase shift around the loop is 0 (or a multiple of 360 degrees)
questions.explanation: The Barkhausen stability criterion for oscillation requires the closed-loop (feedback) gain to have magnitude of exactly 1 and a phase shift of 0 degrees (or an integer multiple of 360 degrees) at the oscillation frequency.

questions.question: A Wien bridge oscillator typically uses which type of feedback network to set its oscillation frequency?
questions.correct_answer: An RC lead-lag network
questions.explanation: The Wien bridge oscillator uses a series-parallel RC lead-lag network that provides zero phase shift and 1/3 attenuation at the oscillation frequency f = 1/(2*pi*RC).

questions.question: LC oscillators such as the Colpitts and Hartley oscillators use resonant tank circuits primarily for:
options: Setting the oscillation frequency via the resonance of the inductor-capacitor combination
Rectifying the AC output to DC
Providing DC bias to the transistor only
questions.correct_answer: Setting the oscillation frequency via the resonance of the inductor-capacitor combination
questions.explanation: LC oscillators rely on the resonant frequency f = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(LC)) of the tank circuit to determine the frequency of oscillation, commonly used for higher radio frequencies.

questions.question: The Colpitts oscillator is distinguished from the Hartley oscillator mainly by:
options: The Colpitts uses a capacitive voltage divider (two capacitors) in the tank circuit, while the Hartley uses an inductive (tapped-coil) divider
The Colpitts uses only resistors for frequency determination
The Hartley oscillator cannot operate at radio frequencies
The Colpitts oscillator requires no active device
questions.correct_answer: The Colpitts uses a capacitive voltage divider (two capacitors) in the tank circuit, while the Hartley uses an inductive (tapped-coil) divider
questions.explanation: In the Colpitts oscillator the feedback is taken from a capacitive divider (two series capacitors), whereas the Hartley oscillator uses a tapped inductor (two series inductors) for feedback.

questions.question: Crystal oscillators are prized for their high frequency stability mainly because:
options: Quartz crystals have an extremely high Q factor and a very stable mechanical resonance frequency
They oscillate at any arbitrary frequency chosen by the user
questions.correct_answer: Quartz crystals have an extremely high Q factor and a very stable mechanical resonance frequency
questions.explanation: Piezoelectric quartz crystals have a very sharp, stable mechanical resonance with high Q, making crystal oscillators far more frequency-stable than RC or LC oscillators.

questions.question: An active low-pass filter built with an op-amp, compared to a passive RC low-pass filter, offers the advantage of:
options: No voltage gain and infinite output impedance
Signal amplification along with filtering and low output impedance
questions.correct_answer: Signal amplification along with filtering and low output impedance
questions.explanation: Active filters use op-amps to provide gain, buffering (low output impedance), and can achieve sharper roll-off, unlike purely passive RC filters which only attenuate and have no gain.

questions.question: The cutoff frequency of a simple first-order RC low-pass filter is given by:
questions.correct_answer: fc = 1/(2*pi*RC)
questions.explanation: For a first-order RC low-pass filter, the cutoff (-3 dB) frequency is fc = 1/(2*pi*RC).

questions.question: A band-pass filter is designed to:
options: Attenuate frequencies outside a specified range while passing frequencies within that range
Amplify high frequencies only, with no attenuation anywhere
questions.correct_answer: Attenuate frequencies outside a specified range while passing frequencies within that range
questions.explanation: A band-pass filter allows a specific band of frequencies between a lower and upper cutoff frequency to pass while attenuating frequencies outside that band.

questions.question: A full-wave bridge rectifier, compared to a half-wave rectifier, provides:
options: Lower output ripple frequency and lower average DC output
Higher ripple frequency (twice the input frequency) and higher average DC output for the same input
Output only during the negative half-cycle
questions.correct_answer: Higher ripple frequency (twice the input frequency) and higher average DC output for the same input
questions.explanation: A full-wave bridge rectifier conducts on both half-cycles, producing an output ripple at twice the input frequency and a higher average DC output than a half-wave rectifier.

questions.question: In a power supply circuit, the purpose of the smoothing (filter) capacitor placed after the rectifier is to:
options: Convert AC to DC directly without a rectifier
Reduce the ripple in the rectified output by charging and discharging to maintain a smoother voltage
Block DC and pass only AC to the load
questions.correct_answer: Reduce the ripple in the rectified output by charging and discharging to maintain a smoother voltage
questions.explanation: The filter capacitor charges to the peak rectified voltage and discharges slowly through the load between peaks, smoothing the pulsating DC into a more constant voltage.

questions.question: A Zener diode voltage regulator maintains a stable output voltage by operating the diode in which region?
options: Cut-off region with no current flow
questions.correct_answer: Reverse breakdown region
questions.explanation: Zener diodes are designed to operate in reverse breakdown, where the voltage across the diode remains approximately constant over a range of currents, providing voltage regulation.

questions.question: A three-terminal linear IC voltage regulator (e.g., 7805) provides a fixed regulated output by:
options: Switching the input on and off at high frequency
Continuously adjusting a series pass transistor to maintain constant output voltage despite input or load variations
Using only a capacitor with no active regulation
Rectifying an AC signal without any DC filtering
questions.correct_answer: Continuously adjusting a series pass transistor to maintain constant output voltage despite input or load variations
questions.explanation: Linear regulators like the 7805 use a series-pass transistor controlled by feedback to continuously regulate and maintain a fixed output voltage against input and load variations.

questions.question: The Boolean expression for the output of a two-input AND logic gate is:
questions.correct_answer: Y = A * B
questions.explanation: An AND gate output is high only when both inputs A and B are high, represented by the Boolean product Y = A*B (or A AND B).

questions.question: A NAND gate's output is the complement of which basic gate's output?
questions.correct_answer: AND gate
questions.explanation: NAND stands for 'NOT AND'; its output is the logical complement (inverse) of a standard AND gate's output.

questions.question: An SR (set-reset) flip-flop is a basic digital circuit used to:
options: Store a single bit of binary information (memory element)
questions.correct_answer: Store a single bit of binary information (memory element)
questions.explanation: A flip-flop is a bistable multivibrator that can store one bit of data, maintaining one of two stable output states (0 or 1) until triggered to change.

questions.question: A D flip-flop, on the active clock edge, transfers the value present at its D input to:
options: The Q output, holding it until the next clock edge
Both Q and its complement simultaneously with different values
questions.correct_answer: The Q output, holding it until the next clock edge
questions.explanation: A D flip-flop captures the input D at the triggering clock edge and transfers it to output Q, holding that value stable until the next active clock edge.

questions.question: A chain of flip-flops connected to divide an input clock frequency and count pulses is called a:
questions.correct_answer: Counter
questions.explanation: A digital counter is built from a chain of flip-flops that sequentially change state with each clock pulse, counting the number of input pulses in binary form.

questions.question: In a 555 timer IC configured in astable mode, the circuit produces:
options: A single output pulse triggered once
A continuous rectangular output waveform (self-triggering oscillator)
questions.correct_answer: A continuous rectangular output waveform (self-triggering oscillator)
questions.explanation: In astable mode, the 555 timer has no stable state and continuously switches between high and low, producing a repeating rectangular (square-ish) waveform without an external trigger.

questions.question: In monostable mode, a 555 timer produces an output pulse of a fixed duration determined mainly by:
options: The frequency of the input trigger only
questions.correct_answer: An external resistor-capacitor (RC) timing network
questions.explanation: In monostable (one-shot) mode, the 555 timer's output pulse width is set by the external RC time constant, approximately t = 1.1*R*C.

questions.question: An analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) is a circuit that:
options: Converts a continuous analogue voltage into a discrete digital (binary) representation
Converts a digital signal into a continuous analogue voltage
Filters out noise from a digital signal
questions.correct_answer: Converts a continuous analogue voltage into a discrete digital (binary) representation
questions.explanation: An ADC samples and quantises a continuous analogue signal, converting it into a digital binary code suitable for processing by digital systems.

questions.question: The resolution of an n-bit ADC (the smallest change in input voltage it can distinguish) improves as:
options: n increases, giving 2^n discrete output levels
The reference voltage increases without limit
questions.correct_answer: n increases, giving 2^n discrete output levels
questions.explanation: An n-bit ADC has 2^n possible output codes; increasing n increases resolution, allowing finer distinction between input voltage levels for a given voltage range.

questions.question: A digital-to-analogue converter (DAC) performs the function of:
options: Converting a digital binary input into a corresponding proportional analogue voltage or current output
Converting analogue signals into binary code
questions.correct_answer: Converting a digital binary input into a corresponding proportional analogue voltage or current output
questions.explanation: A DAC takes a digital code as input and produces an analogue output signal (voltage or current) proportional to the value represented by that code.

questions.question: When a bipolar junction transistor (BJT) is used as a digital switch, it operates by switching between which two regions of operation?
questions.correct_answer: Cut-off (fully off) and saturation (fully on)
questions.explanation: As a switch, a BJT is driven between cut-off (no collector current, acts as an open switch) and saturation (maximum collector current, acts as a closed switch), avoiding the linear active region.

questions.question: Slew rate in an op-amp is defined as:
options: The maximum rate of change of the output voltage per unit time, usually in V/microsecond
The DC gain of the amplifier
questions.correct_answer: The maximum rate of change of the output voltage per unit time, usually in V/microsecond
questions.explanation: Slew rate quantifies how fast an op-amp's output voltage can change in response to a fast input change, limiting large-signal high-frequency performance.

questions.question: Common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR) of a differential/op-amp circuit is a measure of:
options: The amplifier's ability to reject signals common to both inputs while amplifying the difference between them
questions.correct_answer: The amplifier's ability to reject signals common to both inputs while amplifying the difference between them
questions.explanation: CMRR is the ratio of differential gain to common-mode gain; a high CMRR indicates strong rejection of noise or signals appearing identically on both inputs (e.g., interference).
